title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 19: Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec The Party-List System — a Disagreement on Mathematics
keywords: Section 5, Article VI of the 1987 Constitution
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec, the case in which the Supreme Court was united on the constitutional and legal issues of the party-list system but divided on how to convert proportional representation into a mathematical formula.

His rejection of the German Niemeyer formula proposed by Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, on the ground that the Philippine model differs fundamentally in having a three-seat limit and a merely ceiling-like twenty percent allocation, and the Court's 12-3 vote sustaining him and assigning him the ponencia.

The four parameters of the Filipino party-list system that his formula had to respect -- the twenty percent allocation, the two percent threshold, the three-seat limit, and proportional representation -- and the three-step method he crafted around a designated 'first party.'

Justice Mendoza's seven-point Dissent attacking the 'first party' device as judicial legislation and as incapable of consistent and general application, and CJP's replies that the formula merely translated the legal parameters into an equation and that the cure for any perceived unfairness lies in Congress, not the Court.
sub_topics: He opens by stating that Supreme Court decisions form part of the legal system and constitute the final word binding on parties, lawyers, the police, the military, the President and Congress alike.

He notes that once in a while the Court faces dilemmas drawn from other human disciplines, and that Veterans Federation Party was such a case -- a disagreement about mathematics rather than about law.
Justice Mendoza, to whom the case was first raffled, researched parliamentary democracies in Europe and proposed the Niemeyer formula used for the German Bundestag.

CJP objected during the September 2000 deliberations because in Germany all party-list seats must be filled and there is no limit on a party's representatives, whereas the Philippine twenty percent is a ceiling and RA 7941 caps each party at three seats; the Court sustained him 12-3.

The constitutional and statutory background: Section 5, Article VI gives each voter a second vote and leaves the mechanics to Congress; Section 11 of RA 7941 prescribes ranking, the two percent threshold for a guaranteed seat, additional seats in proportion to total votes, and a three-seat maximum.

The 1998 facts: 123 groups participated on May 11, 1998; the Comelec proclaimed thirteen parties (fourteen nominees, including Cocofed's Emerito S. Calderon at 2.04 percent); then, on the petition of thirty-eight defeated groups, the poll body ignored the two percent threshold and filled up all 52 seats.

The three issues framed by the Court: whether the twenty percent allocation is mandatory or a ceiling, whether the two percent threshold and three-seat limit are constitutional, and if so how additional seats should be determined.

The unanimous holdings: the twenty percent allocation is only a ceiling, and the threshold and seat limit are valid, because Congress was 'vested with the broad power to define and prescribe the mechanics of the party-list system'; the Comelec, as a mere implementing body, cannot contravene or amend a statute.

The first rejected proposal -- one additional seat per two percent increment -- discarded because with lopsided votes the three-seat cap would give a party with twenty percent the same seats as one with six percent, contravening proportional representation.

The Niemeyer formula explained and rejected: it too would give all thirteen qualified parties three seats apiece for a total of 39, and it cannot be transplanted because German law discourages small parties while RA 7941 encourages a multiparty system through the three-seat limit.

The four parameters restated, followed by Step One (rank the parties, compute ratios, identify the 'first party'), Step Two (fix the first party's seats, since no other party can exceed them), and Step Three (a complex fraction giving the other qualified parties seats in proportion to the first party's).

The six percent benchmark for the first party -- six percent yields three seats, four to six percent yields two, below four percent yields none -- applied to APEC, which at 5.5 percent received one additional seat for a total of two.

His refusal to round off fractions, resting on Guingona Jr. v. Gonzales and on the principle that whether to round off 'is better left to the legislature,' since 'the Supreme Court does not make the law; it merely applies it.'

Justice Mendoza's seven numbered objections: the rule is applied only to the first party; the law's word 'their' refers to all the two percenters; the remaining seats are a pie to be divided by the two percenters' own weight; there is no basis in the congressional record for a 'first' party; the parameters are internally violated; the result is proportional representation only 'in a Pickwickian sense'; and the scheme makes the twenty percent ceiling improbable to reach.

CJP's one-paragraph refutation in the ponencia -- the formula 'merely translated the Philippine legal parameters into a mathematical equation, no more no less' -- plus two worked examples showing that the simplified equation cancels a common denominator and that non-rounding follows from the three-seat limit.

Justice Puno's Separate Concurrence calling the case 'one of first impression and of immense difficulty' and preferring the majority's geometry as 'more expressive of the spirit of the Constitution, albeit, arguable.'

His closing reflections: that jurists found themselves embroiled in a mathematical problem, that lawyers 'are not, after all, dumb in math,' and that the Court is ready to tackle novel questions raised by new paradigms.

The reproduced Epilogue: the Comelec gravely abused its discretion, arrogated to itself what the Constitution vested in the legislature, and cannot judge the wisdom of an act of Congress; the low 1998 turnout should be a challenge, not a verdict, on the party-list system, Philippine style.
signature_phrases: the Court was united on the constitutional and legal aspects of the case, but was divided on a question of mathematics

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls noticing, when the Niemeyer formula was presented during the Court's September 2000 deliberations, that Germany fills all its party-list seats and caps no party -- and arguing the point until the Court sustained him 12-3 and handed him the ponencia.
He illustrates the transplant problem with the image of growing Washington apples in the Philippines or Guimaras mangoes in the Arctic.
He recounts answering Justice Mendoza's charge that the formula was too strict with a single refuting paragraph inserted into the ponencia rather than a point-by-point rebuttal.
He explains that Mendoza's Dissent quoted only the simplified form of his equation, the full complex fraction having had a common denominator cancelled out as mathematics permits.
He quotes Justice Puno's concurrence admiring both formulas while conceding that 'the fault lies with the inexactitude of the law itself.'
He closes with the wry observation that he never thought jurists would be embroiled in a mathematical problem, consoled that lawyers are 'not, after all, dumb in math.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounts Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec, which CJP presents as a rare case in which the Supreme Court was unanimous on the constitutional and legal questions yet divided on mathematics. After the first party-list election of May 11, 1998, the Comelec proclaimed thirteen qualifying parties and then, on the petition of thirty-eight defeated groups, ignored the two percent threshold to fill all fifty-two seats; the qualified parties in turn sought three seats each. The Court held unanimously that the twenty percent constitutional allocation is a ceiling rather than a mandate, that the two percent threshold and three-seat limit of RA 7941 are constitutional, and that the Comelec, as a mere implementing body, gravely abused its discretion in circumventing the statute. The division came on how to compute additional seats. Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, who had researched European practice, urged the German Niemeyer formula; CJP objected during the September 2000 deliberations that Germany fills all its party-list seats and imposes no cap on a party, while the Philippine system has a ceiling and a three-seat limit, so the formula would again give every qualified party three seats and defeat proportional representation. The Court sustained him twelve to three and gave him the ponencia. His method ranked the parties, identified a 'first party,' fixed its seats by a six percent benchmark, and awarded the other qualified parties additional seats in proportion to the first party's, refusing to round off fractions because rounding could exceed the seats the law allows. Mendoza dissented on seven grounds, chiefly that a rule applied only to the first party is no formula at all and amounts to judicial legislation. CJP answered that the formula merely translated the statutory parameters into an equation and that the cure for any harshness lies with Congress, quoting Justice Puno's concurrence and closing with the Epilogue of his ponencia urging sectoral groups not to despair of the party-list system, Philippine style.
